theme: Sabbath year; the feasts of remembrance
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 15:1-16:22. These chapters deal with the release of debts, the care of the poor, the freeing of slaves, and the three great pilgrim feasts. Notice how generosity is rooted in remembering.
settingTheScene: Moses continues applying the law to life in the land. Chapter 15 describes the Sabbath year, in which debts are released every seventh year, and the freeing of Hebrew slaves. Chapter 16 sets out the three annual feasts: Passover, Weeks, and Booths. These laws shape a community in which no one is permanently poor and every family rejoices together.
observation: “At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release” (15:1).
“But there will be no poor among you… if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD” (15:4-5).
“If among you, one of your brothers should become poor… you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother” (15:7).
“You shall open your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land” (15:11).
“For there will never cease to be poor in the land” (15:11).
Hebrew slaves are to be freed in the seventh year and sent out with gifts: “You shall not let him go empty-handed” (15:12-15).
“You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (15:15).
The three feasts are Passover, Weeks, and Booths, and “they shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed” (16:16-17). Judges are to “follow justice, and only justice” (16:18-20).
interpretation:
The laws in chapter 15 are among the most radical in the Bible. Every seven years, debts are cancelled. The point is to prevent a permanent underclass. In most societies, debt becomes a trap that passes from generation to generation. God’s law builds in a periodic reset.

There is a tension in the passage that is worth noticing. Verse 4 says that there will be no poor among you if you obey. Verse 11 says that the poor will never cease from the land. Both are true. The first is the goal of the law, a society so generous that poverty cannot take root. The second is the realistic observation that because of sin, the ideal will not be fully reached. The command that follows is to open your hand anyway.

The sentence that gives the law its power is 15:15: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you.” Generosity is rooted in memory. The reason the Israelite should free a slave is that he was freed. The reason he gives is that he was given to. The gospel always works this way: we love because he first loved us.

The detail about sending a freed slave away with gifts shows the spirit of the law. He is not just released; he is given a start. “You shall furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress.” Grace is not stingy.

Chapter 16 sets out the pilgrim feasts as occasions of joy. Everyone is to take part: sons, daughters, servants, Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows. And the instruction to judges to pursue justice, and only justice, completes the picture of a society in which God’s character is reflected.
connection: Jesus announced the “year of the LORD’s favor” (Luke 4:19) and taught, “Give to everyone who begs from you” (Luke 6:30). He said, “For you always have the poor with you” (Matthew 26:11), referring to Deuteronomy 15:11. Paul says, “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The church in Acts shared its goods so that “there was not a needy person among them” (Acts 4:34).
application:
Ask whether your hand is open or closed toward someone in need. Make a concrete gift this week.

Forgive a debt or a wrong that someone owes you.

Remember your own redemption, and let it shape how you treat others.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for redeeming you and being generous beyond measure.
Ask him to open your hand to someone in need.
Ask him to teach you to forgive as you have been forgiven.
